t: We Get National Reading Test Results Every 2 Years. Writing? Try 20.
q: Reading and math are important, which is why Congress mandated those tests be given every two years as part of the National Assessment of Educational Progress, known as the NAEP. But writing is equally vital—and not just for success in college and the workplace. Writing can provide powerful boosts to reading comprehension, analytical thinking, and learning in general.

But as the results from NAEP writing tests in 2011 show, American students, on average, don’t write well. Only 27% of eighth- and twelfth-graders scored “Proficient” or above in writing in 2011, an even lower proficiency rate than the one for reading, where it’s hovered at around a third.

But apparently they did. A study found “a pattern of lower performance” on the 2017 writing tests that prevented the release of the results, which were deemed not comparable to those from 2011. A report looking into the 2017 results is still pending.

That, however, is only a problem if you believe you can evaluate those things separately. If, on the other hand, you see them as inextricably intertwined, you come to a different conclusion: The more you can equalize students’ background knowledge of a topic, the easier it is to isolate and measure differences in writing skill.

Giving separate writing tests—and reading tests—also reinforces the widespread and harmful idea that writing and reading comprehension should be taught in isolation from each other and from subjects like history and science. If those aspects of education were better integrated—and if teachers got better training in how to teach them—NAEP scores would almost certainly be much higher than they are, and gaps in scores would be narrower.

Tests like the NAEP can’t address or even identify what’s wrong with our education system. But they can at least sound a general alarm. That alarm rings loudly every two years for reading and math, leading to headlines and rounds of hand-wringing. The hoopla has its downsides, but it’s better than silence.

q: When we pose a question to a class, it is important to provide sufficient Wait Time so that each student has the chance to formulate their response. However, there are a few ways this can go wrong:
The problem is during the Wait Time, that student (and possibly others) were either not doing what was asked of them or were genuinely trying to work out the answer and couldn’t in the time given.
Some students may find it embarrassing to admit they actually tried to answer a question but could not.

I think the answer isn’t about providing more time, but about structuring the time given in the first place. I have tweaked my practice slightly to ensure those few students have every chance to succeed and I believe this has been of benefit to all students.

By instructing students to write down key facts, I am directing their attention to relevant information that can help them answer questions. As with any other classroom routine, I model this technique the first few times so students know exactly what they are expected to do.
In my experience, if given all the tools and facts to work an answer out, students are more likely to attempt the question and even be successful at it.

q: JK — there's no such thing as a lightning fast path to competence. It takes lots of practice. But — but! — there IS something that gets you to competence a heckuva lot faster than most folks: focusing your practice on the work that matters most.

Do you know how to explain things clearly and succinctly? I've seen more than a few highly talented teachers lean too heavily on their verbal acumen — this can feel like productive teaching, but whoever is doing the talking is doing most of the thinking.
But using someone else's complicated system will almost always shortchange you in growth in competence and cost you a lot of time.

Mindless use of strategies. You should seek to add strategies to your tool belt as you work on building competence. But you should never treat the strategy as if it has some inherent power. The power is in the intelligent use of the tool.

q: The trouble is that most teachers in the world overlook one critical word in the strategy: EACH. That word EACH is where the Credibility ground game is won or lost.

t: Credibility Booster: How to Get Better at Authoritative Teacher Presence
q: A major part of such a sense in a teacher's room is teacher credibility — that magic sensation when students in the room believe in their hearts that their teacher is good at their job.
Set your feet hips-width apart. Lynsay says this is especially important for women because "we tend to stand with our feet close together to take up less space.
Be loud. Not obnoxiously so, but, in Lynsay's words, "much louder than most people tend to speak." This projects confidence, and it also ensures that all students can clearly hear you.
Don't end instructions with "Okay?" This makes you sound unsure of the instruction you've just given.

Lynsay recommends first practicing authoritative presence with something you know by heart — e.g., the pledge of allegiance or a memorized poem. This lets you focus on the many components of the skill, not the words that you're saying.

Knowing how to convey an authoritative presence helps in all kinds of life domains, not just the classroom. And, once you develop the habit, it tends to be something you need to think very little about.

t: Why Wordle Works, According to Desmos Lesson Developers
q: The games and stories that have endured longest in our imagination all have a question at their core that is very easy to explain and very hard to fully answer.

Effective feedback attaches meaning to thinking—even and especially incorrect thinking. Expert teachers know that feedback messages like "you're right" and "you're wrong" are less effective than feedback that invites the student who got it right to deepen their thinking and helps the student who got it wrong to see the value in their incorrect answers.
Wordle rewards every thought you bring to it with something new to think about.

The feedback is specific to my response and shows me which parts of my response are useful in the solution and which parts of my response are not useful. The feedback leaves me with actionable next steps.
The same is true with Wordle. Whenever my colleagues trade their answers, they all have the same mystery word, but no two people reached it through the same route of words.
I think one of the most genius moves design-wise was to make it only a single game per day. By doing this, a game that could become addictive and isolating instead brings people together.
Can you offer feedback that goes beyond "right" and "wrong," that helps learners identify everything right about their wrong answers?

t: Not Everyone Needs College, But They Do Need to Learn to Read
q: Manufacturing jobs—the kind that require only a high school diploma but still pay a living wage—have been disappearing fast, despite promises to save them. At the same time, other kinds of jobs are on the increase: ones that pay well and require something more than high school but less than a bachelor’s degree. In 2018, it was estimated that there would be 16 million such openings by 2024, most of them paying more than $55,000 a year, and many paying more than $80,000.

In another indication of the extent of the problem, a former D.C. teacher I know tested all 150 9th graders at a high-poverty school some years ago and found that the average reading level was 3rd grade. High school teachers haven’t been trained to teach basic reading skills, so these students rarely get the help they need.

Even students who have the basics down often can’t decipher words easily enough to achieve reading “fluency,” which is a key factor in comprehension. On national reading tests, 30% of 12th graders score below the “Basic” category, which translates into about 1.35 million students.
It’s not that these students can’t learn to read. If schools used methods supported by scientific evidence, it’s been estimated that 95% of all children could learn to read or “decode” words.

Again, it’s not that these students couldn’t have learned these words. The problem is that schools fail to systematically build knowledge of this kind of vocabulary through content-rich curriculum beginning in the early grades, diving deeply into topics so that kids have the context that will enable them to absorb and retain the words’ meaning.

The long-term solution is to fix our K-12 education system so that it’s no longer turning out so many teenagers and adults who struggling with reading. Unfortunately, the effects of the pandemic are making that dire situation even worse.

The better news is that an increasing number of schools and districts are adopting curricula that provide children with systematic instruction in phonics while simultaneously building sophisticated vocabulary. If we want all students to have a decent chance of success in life—with or without college—we need to do whatever we can to make that approach universal.

t: How I Teach: Cells at KS4
q: I now teach cells in a different way. I am sure I will tweak this method further as time goes on.
By doing this, I try to get the point of cells across. Cells are not random units of life. They have a purpose and everything we will learn about them helps the cell achieve that purpose.

Before I check that students can recall these structures, I say that we use the word organelles to describe them. Next, I conduct a mini-whiteboard quiz and ask students various questions to see if they can recall the names and functions of these 4 organelles.

This is when I describe the function of the nucleus itself: it controls the cell’s activities and it contains the genetic material. In the past, I would also say that it is not the brain of the cell. But by doing this, I have found that I was the one introducing this idea and so I refrain from mentioning it.
At this point, I quiz students again. This tends to be a quick mini-whiteboard quiz, with questions from earlier in the sequence mixed with questions about the new information.

This sequence so far can take more than a lesson. To check understanding, I provide lots of questions, where students can practice recall but also apply their knowledge. These are given both in lesson and as homework.

She starts from the questions students must answer and from what organisms need to survive, so that cells have a purpose.

t: What If School Integration Isn’t The Key To Education Equity?
q: A North Carolina study found that segregation within schools, often known as tracking, accounted for up to 40% of all racial segregation in the state, and it was more common in counties with more integration at the school level. The study also said tracking was more common at higher grade levels.

A third recent study found that more funding goes to Black students than white ones, as well as to poorer kids as compared to wealthier ones. Disadvantaged students also have more full-time teachers and smaller class sizes, although they’re more likely to have inexperienced teachers.
Predominantly Black schools certainly used to get less funding than whiter schools, and some still do. But on average, that no longer seems to be the case.
And yet only 23% of D.C. eighth-graders score at the proficient level or above on national reading tests, nine percentage points below the national average. Racial and income-based gaps are huge.

Children who have access to that knowledge at home, because their parents have more education, end up further advantaged as a result. And teacher-training programs routinely inculcate beliefs that conflict with scientific findings on how kids learn. The kids who still manage to learn are generally those whose families are in a better position to support them.

Well-integrated schools undoubtedly bring benefits, and I hope we have them someday. But integration isn’t necessary to improve education for students from historically marginalized communities and low-income families, nor would it be enough.
x: Integrating a school does not integrate its classrooms, since tracking and ability grouping, including leveled reading, can recreate segregation inside the building.

Recent funding studies suggest disadvantaged students now receive as much or more money on average, and D.C.'s high spending alongside low reading proficiency shows money alone does not raise outcomes.
Wexler questions the common assumption that school integration is the main lever for improving outcomes for Black and low-income students.

She reviews competing studies of 1970s and 1980s integration, notes that those data are over forty years old, and points out that integrated schools can still be internally segregated by tracking and leveled reading.
Wexler locates the real equity lever in curriculum, specifically systematic phonics and content-rich instruction that builds knowledge and vocabulary for children who do not get it at home.
She grants integration may bring benefits but argues it is neither necessary nor sufficient for equity.

t: "I Can't Handle Five Key Beliefs Right Now. Gimme Just One."
q: The strongest place to start creating a more motivation-conducive classroom or school is teacher credibility. If you can move all your students toward believing that you are good at your job, just about everything will move toward becoming easier.

On John Hattie's Visible Learning list, teacher credibility is right near the top, and, if you were to re-order Hattie's list based on an effect-size-to-effort-required ratio, credibility would be on top.
In a given context, signals tell us what kind of story we're in. That's not my language — it's Dan Coyle's in Culture Code. Remarkable cultures rest on just a few skills, according to Coyle.
The story we're telling with Care, Competence, and Passion signals is a really fun one: the teacher in this classroom is good at their job. She knows what she's doing.
Isn't this all kind of overwhelming, Dave? It really can be. But it DOES NOT have to be. Make sure your focus is in spots where you're the sole driver. You'll be so much happier.

t: ‘Now is not a good time’. So when, then?
q: There will always be deadlines and jobs that need to be completed. Even before the pandemic, focusing on improving the quality of our questions or making homework a part of our teaching routine would have taken up thinking and planning time. If it is an important enough focus, then it is worth investing time in it.
When we are stressed, we tend to respond to events automatically, without as much careful thought as when we are not stressed (Hobbiss et al, 2021).
Continuing with our professional development so we focus on improving our practice will prevent us from developing and automating bad habits, and instead promote effective teaching.

The focus (eg. setting routine homework) should have benefits for student learning and needs to be evidence-informed. It really is not a good time (probably ever) if the focus is on extensive written marking or on using a mandated powerpoint format in all subjects.

Talk to staff, really listen to any concerns and take appropriate suggestions on board. The people implementing something new will know better than someone with less teaching time if it can actually be done well.

Teaching is tough job at the best of times, teaching during a pandemic is incredibly stressful and is testing a lot of us. Despite that, there are some things we need to continue doing so we are effective at teaching and have a positive impact on our students’ learning. I would argue that it is, in fact, more important now than ever to improve our practice.

Her reasons are that there is never a perfect time, that improving practice benefits learning, and that stressed teachers revert to automatic and often poor habits, citing research on habit formation.

t: 7 Ways Our Intuition Can Mislead Us About Learning
q: Evidence shows that many or even most kids do need this kind of instruction to become fluent “decoders” of written text—and fluent decoding is key to comprehension. But those who train reading teachers have generally resisted the evidence, and teachers’ intuition about what’s working can be misleading.

At one school I visited, a kindergarten teacher assured me her unsystematic approach to teaching reading was working beautifully. But fifth-grade teachers at the school told me they were shocked to discover many of their students couldn’t sound out simple words like pipe.

But experts can think the way they do only because they have enormous amounts of factual information about their fields stored in long-term memory. Education orthodoxy has frowned on getting kids to acquire factual information, dismissing it as “rote memorization,” but in fact it’s the necessary foundation for critical and analytical thinking.

People do have learning preferences, and there is evidence that it makes sense to convey information in more than one way—using both pictures and words, for example. But if a teacher or student believes that an “auditory learner” just can’t take in information through diagrams—when in fact that’s the most effective way to convey a particular concept—that will only make teaching and learning harder.

Researchers who conducted a series of studies on the effects of print and digital reading found that their subjects—college students—consistently believed they understood more when they read information on a screen. Just as consistently, the evidence showed they actually understood less.

There is in fact a large body of evidence showing that when learners are new to a topic, explicit instruction is far more effective than discovery or inquiry-based learning. But both teachers and students seem to have a bias in favor of the latter approaches, perhaps because they’re more engaging—and it’s easy to mistake engagement for learning.

One thing that’s unlikely to work is shaming people for engaging in practices that don’t line up with science. It’s a natural human tendency to trust our gut feelings—and it’s also natural to become defensive if people tell us we’re being foolish. A better bet is to emphasize shared goals, like ensuring that all teachers and students are as successful as possible.

q: Everest-level goals guarantee the need for course correction. When we pick something to aim at that's far off — something like the long-term flourishing of young people via teaching them to master disciplines with thousands of years of accrued complexity — we're bound to need course corrections as we go.
It's just geometry. When you start at one point and you aim at another that's far away, the likelihood of being able to hit the far away point with a perfectly straight line is really low.
Mastery is an ongoing process — not a checklist or a test at the end of a unit. Doesn't mean get rid of tests or checklists. It just means, this is hard.

I imagine hiking and climbing a great peak is similar. You don't always see clearly where you're heading. Sometimes, the ascent obscures the summit. But the successful mountaineer maintains the course that they intelligently selected when the view was clear.

There's a time to stay the course you previously set, and there's a time to adjust because the course you previously set isn't going to arrive where you want it to. One of the first fruits of wisdom is knowing when to do what.

t: Harvard Has Dropped Its SAT Requirement, But Don’t Expect More Diversity
q: But a recent study of 99 private colleges that adopted test-optional policies between 2005 and 2016 found that the proportion of Black, Latino, and Native American students increased by only one percentage point. The same was true for students from low-income families.

But the SAT, which requires students to analyze complex texts on random topics and understand sophisticated vocabulary, has never assessed innate aptitude alone. To a large extent it actually tests the general academic knowledge that wealthier students are typically better able to acquire, beginning at home.

Instead, instruction during the elementary years focuses on comprehension “skills” like “finding the main idea” rather than content, partly in a futile effort to boost reading test scores. And teachers have long been trained to favor “inquiry” and hands-on projects over direct explanation.
Eliminating or de-emphasizing the SAT and ACT won’t solve the college diversity problem any more than throwing away a thermometer will cure a disease.

The good news is that an increasing number of elementary schools are adopting curricula that teach kids to decipher words and simultaneously build academic knowledge and vocabulary. If students continue to get a knowledge-building curriculum, it’s possible that by eleventh or twelfth grade they will all acquire enough general academic vocabulary to demonstrate their potential on a test like the SAT.

At those grade levels, the best bet is explicit writing instruction embedded in the content of the curriculum and beginning at the sentence level.
